title: Metta's far enemy
hook: ill will is metta's opposite; kindness dissolves it slowly

segments.voice: Yesterday: metta, revisited, and its near enemy, clinging affection. Your line: kindness, not clinging. Today, the enemy that looks nothing like it.

The coworker who chews loudly. The neighbor who parks across your driveway. The relative who always makes that one comment at dinner. Ill will rarely starts big. It starts as an irritation, and then it gets fed: replayed in the shower, told to a friend, rehearsed in imaginary arguments where you always win. After a while, just seeing the person's name can tighten a jaw.
screen: `THE LOUD CHEWER, THE DRIVEWAY.` → `IRRITATION, FED AND REPLAYED.` → `THE JAW TIGHTENS.`

segments.voice: The Visuddhimagga names metta's far enemy plainly: ill will, the Pali vyapada, the wish for someone to suffer. It's called far because it's the opposite of kindness, and easy to recognize. The danger isn't mistaking it. The danger is that it's comfortable, and it grows. So the manual gives a whole toolkit for softening it, one method after another, for when the first doesn't work. One tool: look at what anger does to the one who holds it. The manual compares it to picking up a burning coal to throw at someone: your own hand gets burned first. Another: look for one good quality in the person, even a small one. If their actions are rough, maybe their speech is kind; if not that, maybe their heart has something good in it. The manual compares this to a traveler, hot and thirsty, who finds a pond covered in moss, sweeps the moss aside with his hands, and drinks. Another: everyone is the owner of their own actions; your anger won't fix theirs. One is disarmingly simple: give the person a gift. The manual says a gift can soften a long-held grudge in a moment. And one of the strangest: take the person apart, in your mind, into hair, skin, bones, warmth and breath, and ask, which part am I angry at? It's hard to stay angry at an elbow. None of this is quick. Kindness dissolves ill will slowly, the way water wears down stone. You met the root of this in the Dhammapada's fifth verse: hatred never ends by hatred. Here is the practical how.
screen: `VYAPADA — ILL WILL.` · `THE BURNING COAL.` · `SWEEP THE MOSS AND DRINK.` · `A GIFT, AND WHICH PART AM I ANGRY AT?` · then, large: `ILL WILL SOFTENS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small irritation, one person who annoys you a little, and notice where it lives in your body. Then sweep the moss aside and find one good quality in them, however small: they love their dog, they're kind to the cashier, they work hard. If you can, offer them one breath of the old wish, may you be well, and notice any softening.
Byāpāda. Ill will, the plain opposite of kindness: the manual's tools soften it slowly, one method at a time.
Your line: ill will softens. A whole toolkit, for when the first tool doesn't work. Day two hundred thirty-four, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers draw on the Visuddhimagga's methods for softening resentment, such as recalling a person's good qualities or giving a gift, and practitioners send metta to difficult people in small, gradual steps.
